title: CEFR Multilevel Mock - Speaking - Variant D

parts.title: Part 1
parts.instructions: PART 1 - INTERVIEW (about 3-4 minutes; this timing is the academy's estimate, as no official specification was available). The examiner greets you, checks your name and your identity document, and then asks you twelve short questions in three groups: meals in your day, cooking at home, and food outside the home. Answer in one or two sentences at first, and in more detail as the questions get harder. Answer in English only. You may not prepare notes for this part.

questions.q:
1  EXAMINER SCRIPT - PART 1 (INTERVIEW)

[Examiner, to the candidate:] Good morning / Good afternoon. My name is the examiner for today. Could you tell me your full name, please? Thank you. And could you show me your identity document, please? Thank you. This part of the test lasts about three to four minutes. Please answer in English, and please speak clearly so that the recorder can hear you.

[Say:] I am going to ask you some questions about yourself and about everyday things. There are no right or wrong answers.

CLUSTER 1 - MEALS IN YOUR DAY (about 1 minute)
[Ask ALL four questions, one at a time, in this order. Expect one or two sentences for the first two and a little more for the last two. Do not supply vocabulary. If an answer is a single word, ask once: 'Could you say a little more, please?']
  1. How many meals do you usually have in a day?
  2. What do you normally have for breakfast?
  3. Which meal of the day do you enjoy most, and why?
  4. Has the way you eat during the week changed since you were a child?

CLUSTER 2 - COOKING AT HOME (about 1 minute)
[Say:] Now I would like to ask you about cooking.
[Ask ALL four questions. Expect two to four sentences, with a reason or an example.]
  5. Who does most of the cooking in your home?
  6. Is there a dish that you can cook well?
  7. Do you prefer cooking on your own or cooking with somebody else? Why is that?
  8. What would you like to learn to cook next, and why that dish in particular?

CLUSTER 3 - FOOD OUTSIDE THE HOME (about 1 minute)
[Say:] And now some questions about buying food and eating out.
[Ask ALL four questions. Expect three to five sentences for the last two.]
  9. How often do you eat food that somebody else has prepared?
  10. Where do you usually buy fresh food - at a market, at a supermarket, or somewhere else?
  11. Tell me about a cafe or a restaurant near your home that you would recommend to a visitor.
  12. Do you think food has become expensive in your town? Why do you say that?

[If an answer stops after one word:] Could you explain that a little, please?
[If the candidate misunderstands a question, repeat it once, unchanged, a little more slowly. Do not rephrase it and do not translate it.]

[At the end of Part 1 say:] Thank you. Now we will move on to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.instructions: PART 2 - LONG TURN / CUE CARD (about 3-4 minutes; this timing is the academy's estimate, as no official specification was available). You will be given a topic card about a dish that is often cooked in your family. You have ONE minute to prepare and you may make notes on the paper provided. Then you must talk about the topic for one to two minutes. The examiner will tell you when the time is up and will then ask you two short follow-up questions.

questions.q:
2  EXAMINER SCRIPT - PART 2 (LONG TURN, CUE CARD)

[Examiner, hand the candidate the card, a pencil and a sheet of paper, and say:] Now I am going to give you a topic and I would like you to talk about it for one to two minutes. Before you talk you have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You may make notes on the paper if you wish. Do you understand? Here is your topic card.

--- CANDIDATE TASK CARD ---
Describe a dish that is often cooked in your family.
You should say:
  - what the dish is and what goes into it;
  - when your family usually makes it;
  - who cooks it best, or who taught you about it;
and explain why this dish matters to your family.
--- END OF CARD ---

[Time exactly one minute of preparation in silence. Do not explain vocabulary during this minute.]

[After one minute say:] All right. Remember, you have one to two minutes for this. Do not worry if I stop you. I will tell you when the time is up. Could you start speaking now, please?

[Let the candidate speak. If the candidate stops before one minute has passed, say once: 'Is there anything else you would like to add?' Stop the candidate at two minutes with:] Thank you.

[Then ask BOTH rounding-off questions below and accept short answers of one or two sentences:]
  a) Have you ever cooked this dish for somebody outside your family?
  b) Would you change anything about the way it is made?

[Take the card, the pencil and the notes back and say:] Thank you. Now we will move on to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.instructions: PART 3 - DISCUSSION (about 4-5 minutes; this timing is the academy's estimate, as no official specification was available). The examiner asks you more general questions connected with the topic of Part 2: family meals, learning to cook, health, food and culture, and the future of what we eat. Give full answers, explain your opinion, and support what you say with reasons and examples. You may be asked to compare, to speculate about the future, or to disagree politely with a statement.

questions.q:
3  EXAMINER SCRIPT - PART 3 (DISCUSSION)

[Examiner, say:] We have been talking about a dish that is cooked in your family, and now I would like to ask you some wider questions about food, cooking and the way people eat. Please give full answers and explain your ideas.

[Ask the questions in the order given: they move from the everyday to the general. Use the probe in square brackets only if the answer is short or contains no reason.]

  1. Do families in your country still sit down and eat together at the same table? [Probe: What has made that easier or harder in recent years?]
  2. Why do you think some young people never learn to cook? [Probe: Whose job is it to teach them - the family, or the school?]
  3. What effect has cheap ready-made food had on people's health? [Probe: Can you give me an example you have seen yourself?]
  4. Should schools teach children how to cook and how to shop for food sensibly? [Probe: What would you take out of the timetable to make room for it?]
  5. How do dishes travel from one country to another, in your opinion? [Probe: Does a dish stay the same when it moves, or does it change?]
  6. Some people say that a country's food tells you more about that country than its history books do. Would you agree with that? [Probe: What would a visitor learn about your country from a single meal?]
  7. Is it reasonable to ask people to change what they eat for the sake of the environment? [Probe: And who should pay for that change?]
  8. What do you think people will be eating fifty years from now? [Probe: What makes you think so?]

[General prompts the examiner may use at any point: 'Why do you think that?', 'Can you give me an example?', 'And what about people in the countryside / older people / families with small children?']

[At the end say:] Thank you. That is the end of the speaking test.
